The topic: Fraud Monitoring
Additional context/details: Automated website crawling to combat money laundering.
Source/Reference: PayPal Acceptable Use Policy
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

Automated website crawling is software-based retrieval and examination of web pages. It can support fraud monitoring by comparing publicly displayed merchant activity with information supplied to a payment provider, but it is not synonymous with anti-money-laundering compliance. PayPal's Acceptable Use Policy prohibits specified activities and transactions; its existence does not establish a universal legal mandate to crawl the dark web or a particular detection architecture. Reviewing a merchant's website may help identify prohibited products, misleading descriptions, or inconsistencies requiring further review. A website signal is evidence to assess, not proof of money laundering, dishonest intent, or beneficial ownership. Nor does it replace customer verification, transaction monitoring, investigation, or applicable reporting obligations. Natural Language Processing (NLP), entity resolution, and graph analysis are examples of analytical methods, not confirmed PayPal implementations merely because they could be used. References to FATF, politically exposed persons (PEPs), or Tornado Cash do not by themselves show that the policy requires a named tool, screening system, or cryptocurrency investigation. Collection must also respect applicable law and access restrictions; a security purpose does not grant unrestricted permission to obtain private content. Businesses should understand the relevant Acceptable Use Policy edition, ensure accurate merchant information, and respond to legitimate compliance inquiries. The important distinction is between an illustrative monitoring technique, PayPal's actual contractual restrictions, and legal duties established by the competent regulator.

The topic: Data Portability
Additional context/details: Moving data to another app in machine-readable format.
Source/Reference: GDPR Article
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

GDPR Article 20 provides a qualified right to data portability, not a universal entitlement to transfer every record or an obligation to provide a particular API. It applies to personal data concerning the individual that they provided to a controller when processing is automated and based on consent or a contract. In EDPB guidance, provided data can include observed activity, such as usage records, but not necessarily the controller's inferred profiles or derived analysis. The individual can receive covered data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and transmit it to another controller without hindrance. CSV, JSON, and XML illustrate possible formats; Article 20 does not prescribe those exact formats, OAuth 2.0, real-time synchronization, or a universal API architecture. A readable document is not automatically a suitable portable dataset: practical machine processing and the nature of the data matter. Direct controller-to-controller transmission is available where technically feasible; controllers need not make unrelated systems universally compatible. The right does not apply to processing necessary for a public-interest task or exercise of official authority vested in the controller, and its exercise must not adversely affect others' rights and freedoms. Portability is distinct from Article 15 access and does not automatically erase the source copy; Article 17 erasure has separate conditions. Identify the data, processing basis, automated nature, intended recipient, and feasible format. The point is meaningful reuse and user control, with the statutory scope and safeguards intact, rather than assuming that downloading or transferring data cancels lawful retention duties.

The topic: Daily Working Hours
Additional context/details: 8 hours limit, max 10 hours including overtime.
Source/Reference: Bangladesh Labour Act 2006
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

For an adult worker covered by the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, Section 100 provides the ordinary daily working limit of eight hours, with work up to ten hours subject to Section 108's overtime provisions. The reference is Section 100, not Section 34. The eight-hour ordinary limit should not be described as including an absolute ban on all overtime, while the two additional hours do not create an unrestricted employer entitlement to compel work. Section 102 supplies the weekly framework: ordinarily forty-eight hours, up to sixty hours subject to the statutory conditions, and an annual weekly average not exceeding fifty-six hours. These limits operate together; meeting the daily ceiling alone does not establish weekly compliance. Section 101 addresses rest or meal intervals, and actual working time should be distinguished from the entire spread of attendance. Section 108 requires the applicable overtime premium rather than treating additional hours as ordinary unpaid work. Special rules, lawful exemptions, and the worker's statutory category may affect an individual case, so an unqualified assertion that every imaginable departure is illegal is too broad. Maintain actual start, finish, break, and overtime records, check both daily and weekly totals, and compare the overtime payment with the governing wage components. A contractual clause or time sheet does not itself displace statutory protections, and a breach does not establish an automatic maximum criminal penalty or liability for every later injury without the relevant legal conditions.

The topic: OSH Costs
Additional context/details: Workers should not pay for safety measures.
Source/Reference: ILO Convention 155
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

Article 21 of ILO Convention No. 155, the Occupational Safety and Health Convention, 1981, states the principle that occupational safety and health measures should not involve expenditure for workers. The relevant provision is Article 21, not Article 4, which concerns national policy. The principle addresses financing safety measures, including necessary protective equipment; a compulsory purchase or wage deduction that transfers the expense of an employer's required safety measure to a worker is inconsistent with that allocation. Article 16 supplies related employer responsibilities for safe workplaces, machinery, processes, substances, and necessary protective clothing and equipment, while Article 19 addresses cooperation, information, and appropriate training. Maintenance and proper use of necessary protective equipment are not a reason to shift its safety-related expense onto workers. However, the Convention should not be paraphrased as automatically invalidating every union due, every insurance premium, or every deduction regardless of purpose and domestic law. The actual charge and whether it finances a covered safety measure matter. Nor does Article 21 establish a universal guarantee that all litigation, remediation, or ordinary personal expenses have identical funding rules. National implementation supplies the specific enforcement route and remedies. Identify the required measure, who requires it, the proposed payment or deduction, and the applicable national rules; keep receipts, wage slips, and safety instructions if a charge is disputed. Prevention costs should be allocated without making workers finance the measures intended to protect them.

The topic: Radiation Exposure (Public)
Additional context/details: The annual radiation dose limit for members of the public is 1 mSv per year (compared to 50 mSv for occupational workers), excluding natural background and medical exposure.
Source/Reference: ICRP Publication 103 (2007)
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

ICRP Publication 103 and the IAEA International Basic Safety Standards distinguish planned public exposure from occupational, medical, and emergency exposure. The public effective-dose limit is normally 1 mSv per year for regulated planned exposures. It is not a cap on all radiation a person receives. Patient medical exposure and ordinary natural background are excluded from this public limit, although some controllable natural-source activities have regulatory requirements. Medical exposures require clinical justification and optimization rather than an indiscriminate annual patient cap. Natural background varies substantially; the often-cited worldwide average is about 2.4 mSv per year. Adult occupational effective-dose limits under the international framework are 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years, with no more than 50 mSv in any single year; national law may differ. In specially authorized circumstances, public exposure in one year may exceed 1 mSv only if the five-year average remains no greater than 1 mSv per year. This is not a general allowance for 15 mSv over five years. Effective dose combines organ doses with tissue-weighting factors to support protection planning; it is not an exact individualized prediction of cancer risk. The linear no-threshold model is a prudent basis for protection at low doses, not proof that every small exposure produces a measurable cancer case. Dose limits complement justification and optimization, including ALARA. Emergencies and persistent postaccident exposures use different protective reference levels and decisions; they do not authorize unlimited exposure. Keep routine releases below applicable limits and follow the responsible regulator's requirements.

The topic: Public Education
Additional context/details: Refugees shall receive the same treatment as nationals for elementary education, but only treatment 'no less favourable than aliens generally' for higher education.
Source/Reference: 1951 Convention
Persona: I have high literacy on this topic. Explain the topic according to my level. (High Literacy)

Article 22 of the 1951 Refugee Convention distinguishes elementary education from education beyond that level. For elementary education, Contracting States must accord refugees the same treatment as nationals. For other education, they must provide treatment as favorable as possible and at least no less favorable than that accorded to foreigners generally in the same circumstances. This includes access to study, recognition of foreign certificates, diplomas and degrees, fee and charge remission, and scholarships. Article 22 does not automatically extend its national-treatment clause to all secondary schooling, nor does it limit the second clause only to universities. The relevant educational level and local system must be identified. The foreigner comparison concerns foreigners generally in comparable circumstances, not an absolute right to the best benefit ever offered to any foreign national. Conversely, the Convention does not prohibit a state from treating refugees as favorably as citizens in higher education. It sets minimum protections rather than a ceiling on inclusion. Other human-rights instruments and domestic law may provide stronger educational rights, including for children. Practical access also depends on documentation, language support, and fair recognition processes, but specific accommodations should be distinguished from the express treaty wording. Education helps refugees rebuild their lives and participate in society. Assess the actual admissions, fee, scholarship, and qualification-recognition rules instead of assuming either universal citizen parity or unavoidable exclusion beyond primary school.
